Indonesian free meals agency pledges urgent action to curb food poisoning

Reuters

29 October, 2026 02:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

JAKARTA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – The head of Indonesia’s Nutrition Agency, which runs the country’s free meals programme, said on Thursday that his agency “desperately” needs to prevent food poisoning among the programme’s recipients.

• Sudaryono acknowledged food poisoning was still the main problem to be tackled

• A key campaign promise of President Prabowo Subianto launched in January 2025, the scheme has been marred by a series of problems, including cases of food poisoning and allegations of corruption

Show Full Article

• As of September, at least 57,000 recipients had contracted food poisoning, government data showed

• “We desperately need to solve this immediately so that not a single child is poisoned. That is our top priority,” Sudaryono said at an event

• The rate of food poisoning per one million servings currently stood at 3.6, which was relatively high compared to 0.1 in the United States and 0.8 in Japan, he said

• He said he aimed to bring it in line with the US by strengthening oversight and allowing the agency to monitor CCTV footage from nearly 27,000 kitchens, which would improve worker supervision and hygiene standards

• All kitchens will be forced to purchase seven commodities, including rice, eggs, beef and chicken, on a market platform to be launched by the agency next month, he said

• The platform aims to ensure small farmers and fishermen benefit from the free meals programme, and not just large suppliers

• This year’s budget for the programme was cut by 44 trillion rupiah ($2.42 billion) from 268 trillion rupiah, he said

• The agency has opened 1,460 kitchens in remote areas and areas with high stunting rates, he added

($1 = 18,175 rupiah)

(Reporting by Ananda Teresia; Editing by David Stanway)

Hong Kong leader apologises for deadly Tai Po fire, pledges reforms

Reuters

29 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Clare Jim and Anne Marie Roantree HONG KONG, Oct 29 (Reuters) – Hong Kong leader John Lee apologised on Thursday for the deadly blaze that killed 168 people in the city last November, promising extensive reforms to its building industry and regulatory system.

Lee was speaking shortly before he was due to release a lengthy report by the judge-led panel that is expected to detail a series of regulatory and supervisory failings in Hong Kong’s building-renovation system.

Lee also announced the resignation of Hong Kong’s Housing Secretary Winnie Ho, saying that four government bodies bore partial responsibility.

Show Full Article

Ho was the first official to resign over the inferno. The Hong Kong government, after receiving the committee’s report last week, is expected to decide which individuals and officials, if any, should be held accountable, as well as outlining disciplinary actions and a reform plan.

The blaze that ripped through seven 31-storey tower blocks at the Wang Fuk Court residential complex, which was undergoing renovation work in the northern Tai Po district, was the deadliest in the city since 1948. Thousands of residents were displaced after their homes became uninhabitable.

(Reporting by Clare Jim and Anne Marie Roantree; Editing by Greg Torode, Muralikumar Anantharaman and Saad Sayeed)

Germany’s Steinmeier says China must avoid one-sided benefits in economic ties

Reuters

29 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Liz Lee BEIJING, Oct 29 (Reuters) – In its pursuit of economic self-sufficiency, China must not create one-sided dependence in other markets, Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged in an address at a top-tier university in Beijing on Thursday.

Steinmeier, who will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, was objecting to the trade imbalance between China and Europe, according to his speech text for delivery at the prestigious Peking University.

“It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences,” he said, but pressed that China’s greater independence must not lead to dependence and vulnerability of others on China.

Show Full Article

The European Union has called its widening trade deficit with China unsustainable, and warned last month it will use every possible means to remedy it.

Germany, along with France, has also proposed that the EU enact a new rapid-action measure against countries that harm it, with China likely in focus.

European companies have found themselves with no or little access to the Chinese market, while European markets face large amounts of state-subsidised Chinese imports as well as Beijing’s controls and limits on its raw materials exports, Steinmeier said.

Steinmeier argued that Europe was determined to keep its industrial base, and that he was confident that Brussels and Beijing would be able to find solutions through dialogue.

“We do not want a new bloc confrontation. That would not only be dangerous for international security, but would also be an economic loss for everyone,” said the German president who is on a five-day visit until Saturday.

(Reporting by Liz Lee; Editing by Saad Sayeed)

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92

Reuters

29 October, 2026 12:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Dave Graham MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 (Reuters) – Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, an icon of the Mexican left who took up the banner of the disenfranchised in the 1980s to force changes in the political system despite never winning the presidency himself, has died at 92, the government said on Wednesday.

The first elected mayor of Mexico City, and the son of President Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas shook Mexico’s ruling establishment to its foundations when he ran for the top job in 1988 before losing a hotly disputed election.

That election pitted Cardenas against young technocrat Carlos Salinas, candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which had dominated Mexico since 1929.

Show Full Article

With the two running neck-and-neck on election night, the government suddenly announced the system counting the votes had crashed.

After it came back online, Salinas was declared the winner, although many analysts and Cardenas himself believed the PRI had rigged the vote to retain its hold on power.

The contest was a watershed in Mexico, leading to political reform that strengthened the opposition. Two presidential elections later, in 2000, the PRI was finally ousted.

“His role in Mexico’s contemporary history is fundamental,” said President Claudia Sheinbaum, hailing Cardenas’ impact on Mexican politics.

“In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the desire for change of millions of Mexicans,” she said on social media, alluding to his supporters’ belief that he was the rightful winner of the disputed presidential election.

“That historic election, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation.”

Cardenas ran unsuccessfully for president twice more, fronting a leftist ticket for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which he helped found after breaking with the PRI in 1987. He finished third in 1994 and 2000.

Between those bids, the tall, soft-spoken Cardenas became mayor of Mexico City in 1997, beginning a long run for the PRD at the helm of the capital.

The PRD’s power waned after Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who followed in Cardenas’ footsteps as Mexico City mayor, split from it to found his own Morena party, which became the main force of the Mexican left and propelled him to the presidency.

But Cardenas’ early backing of the PRD marked a turning point in Mexican politics following decades of PRI domination.

It was Cardenas who finally galvanised leftist opposition to the PRI, said historian Lorenzo Meyer, adding, “And he had the capacity to mobilise.”

Cardenas paved the way for subsequent leftist challenges to the highest office, campaigning in remote villages never before visited by presidential candidates.

In later years, he emerged as an occasional critic of Lopez Obrador, a polarizing, often abrasive figure who succeeded him as the standard-bearer of the left and captured the top job in 2018.

Lopez Obrador raised huge protests when he too was denied victory in a bitterly contested presidential election in 2006, and again cried foul six years later. But the dignified Cardenas remained the left’s spiritual leader for many Mexicans.

Cardenas believed free market economics would not save Mexico from economic malaise, favoring a more state-centric model, similar to that later embraced by Lopez Obrador.

COALITION BUILDER

Cardenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, the first year of his father’s six-year term. A champion of land reform who nationalized the oil industry in 1938, Lazaro Cardenas was one of the most popular presidents in Mexican history.

Ironically, the late president’s success helped fortify the PRI, whose legitimacy his son later challenged.

Cardenas earned an engineering degree in 1957, then spent two years in France, West Germany and Italy on a fellowship.

After returning to Mexico, he began a career as a planner and hydraulic engineer, and entered politics in 1976 as a senator for his home state of Michoacan.

As PRI governor for Michoacan from 1980 to 1986, Cardenas was seen by some as too aloof to be a compelling administrator, but his reputation for honesty stood apart from the party’s growing association with graft in the minds of many Mexicans.

Michoacan became a bastion of the PRD, and Cardenas’ son, called Lazaro like his grandfather, also served as governor.

The younger Lazaro later took up senior roles under Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum, preserving the Mexican left’s historic ties with the family.

The challenge to the PRI by Cardenas began in late 1986 when he helped form the Democratic Current within the party.

The Current led calls for the PRI to adopt a more democratic means of selecting its presidential candidate, but these were ignored and leading members left the party in 1987.

“The PRI leadership has stopped our campaign for more open procedures within the party, but we will continue the struggle for true democracy in Mexico,” Cardenas said at the time.

Impressed by his coalition-building skills, newspaper El Financiero once described Cardenas as the sole candidate “who can gather leftist militants, neoliberals, and even ecologists.”

(Reporting by Dave Graham and David Alire Garcia; Editing by Rosalba O’Brien and Clarence Fernandez)
